clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive defect of the OCTN2 sodium-dependent carnitine transporter encoded by SLC22A5, causing urinary carnitine wasting and profound depletion of plasma and tissue carnitine, which starves long-chain fatty-acid oxidation of its obligatory carrier.

Classic presentations are an infantile metabolic form (hypoketotic hypoglycaemia, hepatomegaly, encephalopathy) and a childhood cardiac form with progressive dilated cardiomyopathy and skeletal myopathy; some individuals remain asymptomatic into adulthood.
The hallmark biochemistry is a markedly low plasma free carnitine with low acylcarnitines and an inappropriately high fractional renal excretion of carnitine.
Newborn screening based on low free carnitine can miss an affected infant but may instead flag an affected mother whose own carnitine depletion lowers the baby's screening value.
This is the fatty-acid-oxidation disorder that responds dramatically to lifelong oral L-carnitine supplementation, with reversal of cardiomyopathy and prevention of hypoglycaemic crises.
Untreated disease can cause sudden cardiac death or arrhythmia, whereas treated individuals generally have an excellent prognosis.

Diagnosis rests on very low carnitine that persists despite dietary sources, raised renal carnitine loss, reduced carnitine uptake in cultured fibroblasts and SLC22A5 sequencing, after excluding the far commoner secondary carnitine deficiency.
reference.pathophysiology: OCTN2 is a sodium-dependent transporter that drives active carnitine uptake into the renal tubule, heart, skeletal muscle and other tissues. When SLC22A5 variants impair the transporter, the kidney can no longer reabsorb filtered carnitine, so carnitine is lost in the urine and tissues cannot accumulate it, producing systemic and intracellular carnitine depletion. Without adequate carnitine, long-chain acyl groups cannot be esterified for mitochondrial import, so long-chain fatty-acid oxidation fails; during fasting or intercurrent illness this yields hypoketotic hypoglycaemia and energy deficit, and chronically the heart, which depends heavily on fatty-acid oxidation, develops a dilated cardiomyopathy. Because high circulating carnitine can still drive residual and passive tissue uptake, pharmacological oral carnitine replacement restores tissue carnitine and reverses the functional defect, explaining the excellent treatment response.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary carnitine deficiency from other fatty-acid-oxidation disorders, organic acidaemias, valproate therapy, dietary insufficiency, renal losses or prematurity

redFlags: Dilated cardiomyopathy, heart failure or arrhythmia in a child
Hypoketotic hypoglycaemia with encephalopathy in an infant
An abnormal newborn screen for low free carnitine, whether reflecting the infant or an affected mother
reference.prognosis: With early recognition and lifelong carnitine replacement the prognosis is excellent and the cardiomyopathy typically reverses; untreated disease carries a risk of sudden death.
pitfalls: Labelling the far commoner secondary carnitine deficiency as primary without confirming renal carnitine wasting and genetics
Stopping carnitine once the child is well, after which relapse and sudden death may follow
Missing an affected but asymptomatic mother identified through her infant's screen
Overlooking the diagnosis in unexplained paediatric cardiomyopathy
references: Fatty acid oxidation disorder management consensus guidelines
management: Start lifelong oral L-carnitine supplementation as definitive replacement, which reverses cardiomyopathy and prevents metabolic crises
Avoid prolonged fasting and ensure frequent carbohydrate-rich feeds, especially during intercurrent illness
Manage acute decompensation with intravenous glucose to correct hypoketotic hypoglycaemia during illness
Monitor plasma free carnitine and adjust supplementation and adherence accordingly
Undertake echocardiographic and electrocardiographic surveillance for cardiomyopathy and arrhythmia
Provide genetic counselling and sibling testing for this autosomal recessive disorder, and test the mother when detected through newborn screening
Give the family an emergency sick-day plan and alert documentation
Follow up within a metabolic medicine and cardiology multidisciplinary team
